title: Mohnish Pabrai Presentation and Q&A with UCLA Student Investment Fund - November 5, 2020
summary: Pabrai tells UCLA students how Pabrai Funds began in 1999 as a hobby for eight friends with a cloned Buffett-partnership fee structure and a personal principal guarantee, and how his style has evolved from tech buy-and-hold to 50-cent dollars to, in 2020, a new resolve to hold great compounders past optical fair value. He recounts Satyam and CMGI hundred-baggers, regrets selling Moutai and Ferrari, dismisses sell-side research, and describes the Jack Skeen psychological profiling that told him to sell his company and run a one-person 'single-player math game'.

ideas.idea: Pabrai Funds started in July 1999 as a hobby for eight friends, structured as a Buffett-style 0/6/25 partnership with no management fee, a 6% hurdle and 25% of the profits above it.
ideas.detail: He photocopied pages of a Buffett biography describing the fee structure and had a non-securities lawyer create the LP, later spending a few thousand dollars fixing mistakes. Because the investors were close friends he personally guaranteed their principal and 6% a year; when scaling required dropping the guarantee, he closed the fund and reopened without it and all investors followed.

ideas.idea: Investing his own $1 million from 1994 on Buffett-Munger principles returned more than 70% a year through 1999, taking his net worth to about $10 million before the fund launched.
ideas.detail: The fund was up about 70% after fees in its first year to June 2000, including the NASDAQ crash, because he had completely sidestepped the bubble and owned no Pets.com-type names.

ideas.idea: Someone starting a fund today should keep expenses near zero, run it from home, amortize setup costs over five years, and raise from friends, family and fools, especially the fools.
ideas.detail: He ran the fund from his house for 18 months, then rented one room from his wife's business for about $400 a month with a 10-hour-a-week assistant. A $25,000 legal setup can be repaid by the fund at $5,000 a year. Good performance brings more money and introductions from the initial group, as it did for Buffett.

ideas.idea: Satyam Computer Services was a $10,000 bet in the mid-1990s that became about 140x because it traded below the liquidation value of its Hyderabad real estate while growing 50% a year with Fortune 500 recurring revenue.
ideas.detail: He knew the company through shared US clients. He sold within two weeks of the 2000 peak when a spun-out dotcom subsidiary inflated the valuation; the stock then lost 60-70%.

ideas.idea: CMGI, a Boston incubator spawning dotcoms, was bought at a modest valuation as a way to own the internet without knowing which company would win, and a $100,000 10% bet became over $10 million.
ideas.detail: He compares it to owning Tencent or Alibaba today: businesses that throw many things at the wall, most of which don't stick, but the ones that do stick do very well.

ideas.idea: In bubbles the market splits in two: a frenzied sliver and boring businesses nobody wants, and the day the NASDAQ peaked in March 2000 Berkshire hit a multi-year low; today (2020) looks somewhat similar.
ideas.detail: Berkshire was around 40,000 down from 70,000 as the NASDAQ hit 5,000. In 2020 he sees a small sliver that is egregiously overvalued, a large portion probably overvalued but not egregiously, and many businesses people aren't interested in.

ideas.idea: The big epiphany of 2020 is that if you were lucky enough to buy a great compounder with a long runway at a reasonable price, do not sell it just because it reaches 100 or 120 cents on the dollar; hold until it is egregiously overvalued.
ideas.detail: He calls 2020 his biggest learning year since the mid-1990s. For 20 years he had bought 50-cent dollars and sold at 90 cents, a fine 20%-plus return but one that requires constantly finding the next idea and paying taxes; the better model is to stay on the train and get off only when it gets egregious.

ideas.idea: Munger won't sell Costco at 40 times earnings even though he wouldn't buy it there, admitting there is no intellectual way to justify it; give great businesses with intact DNA room to run.
ideas.detail: From a socially distanced dinner on Munger's LA patio a week earlier. Pabrai guesses Munger would hold Costco at 50 or 60 times but not at 100 or 200. Costco has one store in China and is in a small number of countries, so outcomes include a thousand-plus Chinese stores.

ideas.idea: He is not wired to pay up for a great business, so his universe is compounders that are unrecognized or hit by a temporary hiccup and therefore cheap, but with a genuinely long runway.
ideas.detail: Other investors are wired to pay up and that is fine for them; he is limited to buying the growing pie cheap and then, unlike in the past, running it for a while. Finding one or two such ideas a year is plenty.

ideas.idea: Selling Moutai after a 6-7x because it looked optically expensive at a high-20s/low-30s multiple was a mistake; it more than doubled afterward and will keep going.
ideas.detail: Moutai is the most valuable liquor company on the planet at over $200 billion market cap, with a cost of goods of about $5 per bottle sold for $150 and pricing power to reach $300 or $500. Volume is constrained by local sorghum acreage and a single annual water draw at the autumn full moon; 80% of Moutai sold in China is counterfeit.

ideas.idea: Selling Ferrari at $70-100 a share when it looked expensive on trailing earnings was another mistake; it has more than doubled since, and it has never spent a dollar on advertising in 70-plus years.
ideas.detail: Ferrari came public via the Fiat Chrysler spin-out in the $40s around 2016 and the position exceeded $100 million. Neither Moutai nor Ferrari was egregiously overvalued, only optically so for a cheapskate; as Munger says, we are old too soon and wise too late.

ideas.idea: From 2020 onward he is no longer interested in discounted dollar bills; the pie has to be a growing pie, bought cheap and then held.
ideas.detail: He hopes to have 25-35 more years of runway to apply the lesson of 2020 rather than repeat the Moutai and Ferrari exits.

ideas.idea: Sell-side research is mostly garbage because analysts focus one or two quarters ahead and set price targets only 30-40% above the current price, ratcheting up as the stock rises.
ideas.detail: A Mumbai broker's report valued Satyam at 60 rupees when it was 40, though its real estate alone was worth twice the price and the business was growing 50% a year; the analyst told him a 600-rupee target was not allowed. Owners don't need next-quarter precision, only long-term trajectories and probabilities.

ideas.idea: Useful idea sources are Value Investors Club, SumZero and thoughtful write-ups people email him, because buy-side authors actually want to own the businesses.
ideas.detail: Sell-side material is only for entertainment; these venues contain somewhat thoughtful write-ups.

ideas.idea: He would rather invest in the US, where governance and language are easier, and the hurdle for overseas investments is higher, but his portfolio is full of foreign names simply because that is where value is.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Overseas he has to meet the company and get past language and cultural issues to understand the nuances. In 2020 he found only one US business to buy, during the April-May COVID selloff; most recent finds have been outside the US.

ideas.idea: Humans arrive without an owner's manual; who you are is hard-coded by genetics and the first five years, so align your outer map to your inner map rather than conform to the world.
ideas.detail: Two industrial psychologists (firm named Conquest, after Genghis Khan, who was a tyrant inside and out and therefore effective) tested him in 1999 with 360 interviews and produced a 20-page personality template he rereads every year. Their advice: don't try to be Gandhi outside if you're a villain inside.

ideas.idea: The profiling told him to get rid of his 160-employee IT company within six months because managing people was off his map, and that his calling was a single-player mathematical game he believed he could win, which is exactly what Pabrai Funds is.
ideas.detail: He loved the business for its first four or five years when it was a math game of leads and closes, and hated it once his role became managing politics among vice presidents. Two of the psychologists each invested $100,000 in the fund, saying 'I cracked your brain open, I know exactly what's in there'. He recommends everyone get their manual (about $10,000 a person now versus $25,000 for 12 people then) and have the intestinal fortitude to read it.

ideas.idea: Keep the team size at one: 21 years in, Pabrai Funds is as exciting as day one because the numbers got larger but the team never did.
ideas.detail: The psychologists told him he does not do well in team sports; he plays bridge four or five hours a week (Buffett plays 10-12) as a near-single-player math game, and investing is a rational, analytical game of the same kind.
